text:
Pre-requisites
The following items are pre-requisites for following all of the activities:

Have R and RStudio up and running. A ‘how-to’ guide is available here: https://rstudio-education.github.io/hopr/starting.html.
Have a free GitHub. * Sync GitHub and RStudio. Some resources to help you do this are available at:

https://happygitwithr.com/rstudio-git-github
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2QJQ6pNroVM



Basics of computational reproducibility concepts
Most of this workshop assumes that participants are already familiar with the basic project- and folder-based working scheme, including how to organise code, data, and other project files within a clearly defined project folder. Although the examples in this workshop use RStudio, this approach is not specific to RStudio or even to R. The same principle can be applied when working with other development environments and tools, such as Visual Studio Code, Jupyter Notebooks.
Keeping the code, configuration files, dependencies, and other relevant project files together in a well-defined structure makes it easier to understand how an analysis was produced, share it with others, move it between computers, and recreate it in the future. More on this is available here.

title: 1  R packages version management with renv
text:
1.1 Why do I need renv?
Remember the time when you opened an old R project and found that the code no longer runs because packages have been updated or changed?
This is where renv comes in handy. It helps you keep track of the exact R packages and versions that your project depends on, creating a project-specific environment that can be shared and recreated by others. By recording these dependencies in an renv.lock file, renv makes it much easier to come back to a project months or years later, or for someone else to run your analysis and get the same results. In that sense, renv is a really useful part of making R projects more reproducible and easier to share. Further details from the official resource are available here here.
crumbs: 1  R packages version management with `renv`

title: 1  R packages version management with renv
text:
1.2 How is this done?
Think of renv as creating a private package environment for each R project. In the background, it works roughly like this:

You initialise the project (with renv::init()). renv creates an renv/ folder and sets up a project-specific library where packages for that project are stored.
Next, you install packages normally, e.g. install.packages(“dplyr”), alternatively you can use renv::install(), which is shorter and can install packackes beyond official repositories, e.g. not just CRAN but from GitHub. Instead of relying only on your computer’s global R library, renv keeps the project’s packages isolated. So, you will not see or have available packages that you have not install for this specific project.
Then, renv tracks what the project uses. When you run renv::snapshot(), it examines the project and records the packages, versions, and sources in a file named renv.lock. This is the imporant bit. The lockfile becomes the reproducibility record. Someone cloning your Git repository can run renv::restore(). renv reads renv.lock and installs the specified package versions into that project’s private library.
Having project-dedicated packages doesn’t mean duplicating the space used for packages installed. renv uses a global package cache on your computer. Rather than keeping completely separate copies of every package for every project, project libraries can link to packages in this cache. This saves disk space while still keeping projects isolated.

The diagram below illustrates most of this process.
crumbs: 1  R packages version management with `renv`

title: 1  R packages version management with renv
text:
1.3 Instructions

1.3.1 Create a new RStudio project linked to GitHub
To create a new RStudio project with GitHub version control, first create an empty repository on GitHub (Guidance if needed is here). Then, in RStudio select File -> New Project -> Version Control -> Git and paste the repository URL to clone it to your computer (The url looks something like: https://github.com/yourusername/my-r-project.git).
RStudio will create the local project and connect it to the GitHub repository as a remote. From then on, you can use RStudio’s Git pane to stage changes, commit them with a message, and push them to GitHub, while pulling changes made by others.


1.3.2 Set your package source repository and date
R package repositories are online servers that host R packages and their different versions. CRAN is the default repository most R users rely on, but the versions available there change over time as packages are updated.
For reproducible projects, it is useful to explicitly set the repository to a specific date, so that installing the project later retrieves packages from the same snapshot of the repository (it is like travelin in time!). For this activity, use Posit Package Manager and fix it to 6 September 2026. Run the following code before installing any packages (you can do this from the R console:
options(
  repos = c(
    "CRAN" = "https://packagemanager.posit.co/cran/2026-09-07"
  )
)
This tells R to use the specific snapshot repository rather than the most up-to-date defaul repository. If you also need a package that is not available from CRAN, there are ways to do it, e.g. the rOpenSci R-universe repository.
If you run getOption("repos") again, you should see the URLs you have entered above. If it is set, the package versions you install will always correspond to the date you used. The date can be change to use more updated packages if desired.


1.3.3 Install {renv}
First, install the package from CRAN using install.packages().
# Install renv (only needed once)
install.packages("renv")
You only need to do this once on your computer. Then initialise the environment from within your project; this creates a project-specific library and sets up the files needed for renv to manage your R package environment.
# Initialise renv for the current RStudio project
renv::init()
Your console output will display something like the below:
The following package(s) will be updated in the lockfile:

# CRAN -----------------------------------------------------------------------
- renv   [* -> 1.1.1]

The version of R recorded in the lockfile will be updated:
- R      [* -> 4.4.3]

- Lockfile written to "path-to-your-project/renv.lock".
- renv activated -- please restart the R session.
With this, renv will scan your project, identify the packages it currently uses, and create an renv.lock file containing information about their versions and sources. It is a good practice to commit this file to GitHub as you add more packages.






Important



Restart your R session so that {renv} can take effect. In RStudio, go to Session -> Restart R. After restarting, R will load the project with the new {renv} environment active.
Do not skip this step!! as the following commands rely on {renv} being initialised correctly.




1.3.4 Customize the {renv} configuration
Before continuing, you need to set up how renv will do a few things.
By default, {renv} scans your R scripts to identify which packages your project uses and records them in renv.lock. However, it can miss packages that are loaded in less obvious ways. To avoid missing dependencies, we can tell {renv} to track all packages installed in the project, instead of trying to guess which ones are used.
To do so, run the following in the R console:
renv::settings$snapshot.type(value = "all")
Also, we have already configured R to use Posit Package Manager above. We should also tell {renv} to use it when managing packages. To do so, run this in the R console:
renv::settings$ppm.enabled(value = TRUE)
This helps keep package installation consistent with the repository and snapshot date defined earlier.


1.3.5 Installing packages
We will install the packages needed for the various parts of the workshop using the code below:
# list packages used in project
packages <- c(
  'targets', 
  'usethis', 
  'visNetwork',
  'dplyr',
  'readr',
  'sf',
  'yaml',
  'ggplot2'
)
# install/update packages
install.packages(packages)

# Do not run
# Example of additional packages installed outside CRAN
# renv::install("https://github.com/urbanbigdatacentre/AccessUK")
The R console will display a list with the packages and versions that will be installed. It will also promt the question Do you want to proceed? [Y/n]:. Agree and wait for the packages and their dependencies to be installed.


1.3.6 Let’s take a snapshoot of this!
The next important thing is to keep a record of the packages as you continue to work, saving all the details to be recovered if you come back to this later or share your code with someone.
First, you can check how what is being kept at the moment by running the following:
renv::status()
You will see that the recently installed packages are installed but not recoded in your renv. The report looks something like this:
The following package(s) are in an inconsistent state:

package     installed recorded used
backports   y         n        y
dplyr       y         n        y
.
.
.
.
readr       y         n        y
sf          y         n        y
vctrs       y         n        y

See `?renv::status` for advice on resolving these issues.
After checking the project status, use renv::snapshot() to record the current package versions in renv.lock. This makes sure that the project’s current package environment can be reproduced later using their same version, etc.
renv::snapshot()
Some times some dependencies will have to be installed manually. You knwo this as there will be some warning. If so, install the missing package(s) and then run renv::snapshot() again.
Then check the status again:
renv::status()
If everything is set up correctly, renv::status() must show the following message:
No issues found -- the project is in a consistent state.


1.3.7 Commiting to GitHub
Once renv::status() reports that the project is consistent, commit the changes to GitHub using RStudio’s Git pane.
The important file here is renv.lock. It records the exact package versions needed to recreate the project’s R environment. The installed package library is not committed because renv automatically adds it to .gitignore.
In RStudio, open the Git pane, usually located in the top-right panel. You should see a list of files that have changed since your last commit. Look for renv.lock.
You may also see other project files that you have created or modified. Tick the Staged checkbox next to the files you want to include in the commit.
A new window will open showing the files being committed. Enter a short message describing the changes, for example: Set up reproducible R environment with renv Then click Commit.
Back in the Git pane, click Push. RStudio will upload your new commit to the remote GitHub repository.
You can then check the repository on GitHub and confirm that renv.lock is there.


1.3.8 Restoring an environment{restore-environment}
Now let’s test whether the project can actually be recreated from the renv.lock file. The idea is to pretend that you are opening the project on a new computer, where the required packages have not yet been installed.
The easiest way to do this is to make a copy of your project and use that copy for the test. Make sure the copy contains your project files and the renv.lock file, but do not copy the existing renv/ folder. We want renv to install the packages again from the lockfile instead of simply using the packages that are already installed.
Open the copy of the project in RStudio. If renv is not already installed, install it with:
install.packages("renv")
Then initialise renv:
renv::init()
If renv detects the existing renv.lock file and asks whether you want to use it, choose Yes.
Now restore the project environment:
renv::restore()
{renv} will read the package versions recorded in renv.lock and install them into the project’s new renv environment. Specifically, renv attempts to recreate the versions that were recorded when the project was saved, not the most up-to-date or any other available version by default.
You may see a message similar to:
The following package(s) will be installed:

# CRAN -----------------------------------------------------------------------
- dplyr   [1.1.4]
- readr   [2.1.5]
- sf      [1.0-21]
- vctrs   [0.6.5]
- units   [0.8-7]

Do you want to proceed? [y/N]:
Enter y and press Enter to proceed.
Once the restoration has finished, check the project again:
renv::status()
If everything has been restored correctly, renv should report that the project is consistent with the lockfile.
This gives you a useful test: if the project works after starting with the renv.lock file and restoring the packages, you can be more confident that someone else will be able to recreate the same R environment on their computer.


1.3.9 Limitations
Of course, renv isn’t a complete solution to reproducibility (as perhaps any individual tool). It mainly captures the R package environment, but your results can also depend on the R version, operating system, system libraries, external software, and data. Some packages may also become unavailable or difficult to install in the future. This is why it can be useful to combine renv with tools such as targets to make the step-by-step analysis systematic and clear, and Docker or Binder to capture the wider computing environment and make it easier for others to run the project in a consistent setup.

title: 2  Analysis pipelines with targets
text:
2.1 Why do I need targets?
Have you ever had to re-run an entire analysis from the beginning because you changed one input file or modified a single step in your code? or, have you came across a code-based project developed by someone else, and you don’t know where to start?! This can become particularly frustrating when some parts of the analysis take a long time to run or when a project consists of many scripts that need to be executed in a particular order.
This is where {targets} comes in handy. It helps you organise an analysis as a pipeline of connected steps, where the output of one step becomes the input of another. targets keeps track of these relationships and knows which parts of the analysis need to be re-run when something changes. This makes complex analyses easier to manage, update, and reproduce, while avoiding unnecessary computation.
For those with Python experience, this very similar to Snakemake.
crumbs: 2  Analysis pipelines with `targets`

title: 2  Analysis pipelines with targets
text:
2.2 How is this done?
Think of targets as turning your analysis into a map of connected tasks. You define the main steps of your workflow—such as importing, cleaning, analysing, and visualising data—and specify how they depend on each other. targets then builds a dependency graph of these steps, so it knows what needs to be run and in what order.
You run the pipeline with targets::tar_make(). {targets} checks what has changed since the last run and re-runs only the steps affected by those changes, rather than running the whole analysis from scratch. This makes the your work more efficient and, importantly, makes the logic and dependencies of your analysis explicit and easier for others (or your future self) to understand and reproduce.
crumbs: 2  Analysis pipelines with `targets`

title: 2  Analysis pipelines with targets
text:
2.3 Instructions
Overview: In this part, we will create a pipeline with some spatial functions which will in the end create a reproducible map showing accessibility by public transport to employment in Glasgow Region. To do so, we will follow the following conceptual steps.

Download accessibility data (Pre-computed accessibility indices by public transport)
Download spatial data (Administrative boundaries in Scotland callde Data Zones)
Process and join data
Generate map


2.3.1 Getting ready
Continue working in your RStudio project where you left it. Alternatively, if you did have time to finish it, you can pick it up where we leave by downloading a copy of the repository from here (click on the green botton that say ‘Code’ and then download). If you download it, then restore the environment following the instructions here.
Before moving forward, just check that the packages needed are there running:
renv::status()
{renv} should report that the project is consistent with the lockfile.


2.3.2 A {targets} pipeline structure and an example
A {targets} pipeline is organised around a special _targets.R file, which acts as the blueprint for your analysis workflow. Inside this file, you define a series of targets (the individual steps of your analysis) and how they depend on one another. A typical pipeline might move from reading/downloading data -> cleaning/processing data -> analysing/modelling data, with each step becoming a target that {targets} can track and re-run when necessary.
To see what a basic {targets} project looks like, you can let the package create a small template for you including a toy pipeline example:
targets::use_targets()
This creates the basic files and folders needed to get started, including _targets.R file in your root directory.


2.3.3 Exploring how {targets} works
Let’s explore how {targets} represents the different steps and their dependencies. Start by opening the _targets.R which was created in the root directory and looking at the example that was just created.
You can visualise the pipeline with:
targets::tar_visnetwork()






Note



When you run targets::tar_visnetwork(), you may be prompted to install the visNetwork package, which is used to display the pipeline as an interactive network.
If prompted, follow the instructions to install the package. Once it has been installed, remember to run renv::snapshot() so that the new dependency is recorded in your renv.lock file.


This opens a diagram showing the targets in your pipeline and the relationships between them. Take a moment to explore the diagram and see how the different steps are connected.
Next, run the pipeline:
targets::tar_make()
tar_make() executes the targets in the order oulined in the list, based on their dependencies. A folder called _targets is created in the root directory. You can access these files and check for intermediate steps. You can learn more here.
Once it has finished, run targets::tar_visnetwork() again and explore the differences. This helps to understand how {targets} keeps track of the workflow and its outputs.
Delete saved outputs of all or certain steps, run:
targets::tar_destroy()
To delete the saved results of steps that you might have deleted and will not use anymore, you could run:
targets::tar_prune()


2.3.4 Setting _targets for our own analysis
You can simplify the _targets.R file by removing most of the explanatory comments muted with the hastag, particularly those describing the available target options. For this tutorial, we recommend keeping the configuration simple and setting the default storage format to qs:
tar_option_set(
  format = "qs"
)
The ‘qs’ format is a faster and more space-efficient alternative to the standard rds format. This is the format that targets will use to save the output of each target unless you explicitly use format = "file" or specify a different format within an individual tar_target().
It is also recommened removing the packages option from tar_option_set() and instead specifying the packages required by each tar_target() individually. This makes the pipeline more efficient and robust as each target only loads the packages it actually needs, reducing overhead and potential conflicts. For more configuration options, see the tar_option_set() documentation.
### Step 1 and 2 in our analyses
The recommended workflow is that you organise the your work with custom R functions. For instance, the first thing we need to do is download data.
For this, create a in simple empty R script called 01_utils.R and save it in the R/ folder (create it if you don’t have one).
First we want to start by downloading the accessibility data using some code such as:
dir.create("./data/raw", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
url_data <- 'https://huggingface.co/datasets/rafavdz/accessibility-indicators-2023/resolve/main/records/employment_all/access_employment_all_pt.csv'
file <- paste0("./data/raw/", basename(url_data))
  
download.file(
  url = url_data,
  destfile = file,
  mode = "wb"
)
We will wrap this steps in a function. So, in your 01_utils.R, write the following:
# Download accessibility data
download_accessibility <- function() {
  dir.create("./data/raw", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  url_data <- 'https://huggingface.co/datasets/rafavdz/accessibility-indicators-2023/resolve/main/records/employment_all/access_employment_all_pt.csv'
  file <- paste0("./data/raw/", basename(url_data))
  
  download.file(
    url = url_data,
    destfile = file,
    mode = "wb"
  )
  
  return(file)
}
This data contains the accessibility levels for each cesus area in Great Britain (LSOA in England and Data Zone in Scotland).
Additionally, we will need the spatial data repsenting each of the Data Zones in Scotland. Then, write the following function in 01_utils.R:
# Download data zone geometries in Scotland
download_datazone <- function() {
  dir.create("./data/raw", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  
  zip <- "./data/raw/SG_DataZoneBdry_2011.zip"
  dir <- "./data/raw/datazones_scotland"
  
  download.file(
    "https://huggingface.co/datasets/rafavdz/datazones_scotland2011/resolve/main/datazones_scotland.zip",
    zip,
    mode = "wb"
  )
  
  dir.create(dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  
  unzip(zip, exdir = dir)
  file.remove(zip)
  
  shp_path <- list.files(
    dir,
    pattern = "\\.shp$",
    recursive = TRUE,
    full.names = TRUE
  )
  
  return(shp_path)
}

2.3.4.1 Setting the new functions and targets to download data
Now, you have some download functions, which you can define by specifying the it in the _targets.R file as following:
tar_source(
  "R/01_utils.R"
)
This will run the R scripts in the R/ folder with your custom functions.
Now, you can specify two targets in the list as following:
# target list
list(
  # 1. Download accessibility data
  tar_target(
    name = access_data,
    command = download_accessibility(),
    format = "file" 
  ),
  # 2. Download spatial data
  tar_target(
    name = datazone_scotland,
    command = download_datazone(),
    format = "file" 
  )
)
As you can see, each target follows a simple structure. The name gives the target a unique name, which is how you refer to its output in subsequent targets. The command specifies what should be run to create that target—in this case, a function. You can also include arguments within the function call when needed, and specify packages required by a particular target, although we do not need to do this yet.
Notice that we have set format = "file" for both targets. This tells targets that these commands produce files, rather than R objects, and allows targets to track those files as part of the pipeline.


2.3.4.2 Running download targets
Now that the two download targets have been defined, let’s check how they appear in the pipeline and then run them. First, use targets::tar_visnetwork() to explore the dependency graph and confirm that both targets are included. Then run the pipeline with:
targets::tar_make()
{targets} will execute the two download functions and save the resulting files in the locations specified by those functions. Once the pipeline has finished, explore the data/ folder in your project. You can then run targets::tar_visnetwork() again to see that the targets have been completed and that their outputs are now being tracked by {targets}.



2.3.5 Step 3 - Processing spatial data
Now you have a sense of the logic in targets. We will move on to the processing of the data that we just downloaded. To do so, create a create a in simple empty R script within the R/ folder called 02_processing.R.
In this R file we will write our processing flow (simple for the sake of example but with various spatial operations):
# Fun process accessibility and spatial data
process_access <- function(access_data, datazone_scotland) {
  
  # Read data
  accessibility_indices <- readr::read_csv(access_data)
  datazones <- sf::st_read(datazone_scotland) |> 
    st_transform(27700)
  
  # Glasgow city centre
  glasgow_cc <- sf::st_point(c(-4.256300, 55.860484)) |>
    sf::st_sfc(crs = 4326) |> 
    sf::st_transform(27700)
  
  # Subset
  datazones_glasgow <- datazones |> 
    sf::st_filter(st_buffer(glasgow_cc, 10e3)) 
  
  # Join accessibility data to Glasgow
  datazones_glasgow <- datazones_glasgow |> 
    left_join(accessibility_indices, by = c('DataZone' = 'geo_code')) 
  
  # Return SF Glasgow with access data
  return(datazones_glasgow)
}


2.3.6 Step 4 - Modelling or creating ouputs
The step above subset and joins the data to the geometry. From here, we can continue modelling or excutening further analysis. For this example, we will create a static map. So, in the 02_processing.R, include the following function, too:
# Create accessibility map
plot_employment_access <- function(accessibility_sf){
  # Output directory
  dir.create(
    "./data/generated",
    recursive = TRUE,
    showWarnings = FALSE
  )
  
  # Output filename
  output_file <- "./data/generated/accessibility_map.png"
  
  # Create map
  map_ggplot <- accessibility_sf |>
    dplyr::filter(time_of_day == "am") |>
    ggplot2::ggplot() +
    ggplot2::geom_sf(
      ggplot2::aes(fill = access_employment_all_45 / 1e3),
      linewidth = 0
    ) +
    ggplot2::labs(
      title = "Accessibility to employment",
      subtitle = "Travel time by public transport at morning",
      fill = "Jobs \n(In thousands)"
    ) +
    ggplot2::scale_fill_viridis_b(n.breaks = 6) +
    ggplot2::theme_void()
  
  # Save map
  ggplot2::ggsave(
    plot = map_ggplot,
    filename = output_file
  )
  
  # Return filename so targets can track the file
  output_file
  
}
Note that it is a good practice to keep util, processing (and potentially other types of tasks), in separate files. Also, it is a good idea to keep some sequential numbering.


2.3.7 Excecuting the full pipeline
Following the logic above, what the next step?…
That’s right! We will specify where the next function lives, and create new targets in the list. For the first part adjust the code to let target know about the new functions:
tar_source(c(
  "R/01_utils.R", 
  "R/02_processing.R"
))
Then, expand the targets list with the Step 3 and 4 as following:
  # 3. Process and join data
  tar_target(
    name = subset_glasgow,
    command = process_access(
      access_data = access_data,
      datazone_scotland = datazone_scotland
    ),
    packages = c("dplyr", "readr", "sf"),
    format = "qs"
  ),
  # 4. Generate map
  tar_target(
    name = accessibility_map,
    command = plot_employment_access(
      accessibility_sf = subset_glasgow
    ),
    packages = c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "sf"),
    format = "file"
  )
The next two targets extend the pipeline by processing the downloaded data and then producing a final map. The ‘subset_glasgow’ target runs process_access() using the outputs of the two previous targets (‘access_data’ and ‘datazone_scotland’), so {targets} knows that these data must be available before this step can run.
It also specifies the R packages required for each of these particular steps. The resulting object is stored using the ‘qs’ format. The ‘accessibility_map’ target then takes subset_glasgow as its input and passes it to plot_employment_access() to create the map. Here, ‘format = “file”’ tells {targets} that the output is a file rather than an R object, allowing it to track the generated map as part of the pipeline.


2.3.8 Build the full pipeline
Before runnig the extented pipeline, visualised it using targets::tar_visnetwork(). This should map where you are at the moment with the analysis, e.g. downloaded the data, there are new functions, new outcomes, but some of these are outdated.
Now, run the targets with targets::tar_make(). This should only excecutre the outdated targets. Crucially, it should generate our accessibility map as following:

If for some reason, something didn’t go well or there was not enough time to complete this activity, you can download the complete activities from this repo. You should be able to quickly restore the renv, and the, simply run target::tar_make().
crumbs: 2  Analysis pipelines with `targets`

title: 2  Analysis pipelines with targets
text:
2.4 Limitations and next steps
Taken together, renv keeps track of the exact packages we need, while targets makes the steps of our analysis clear. But there is still a bit more going on behind the scenes. Our results can also depend on the version of R we are using, the operating system, system libraries, etc. Docker allows us to capture this wider computing environment in a reproducible container. In the next chapter, we will see how Docker and Binder can bring these pieces together and make the whole workflow easier for others to reproduce.
crumbs: 2  Analysis pipelines with `targets`

title: 3  Containers: Your own Git repository reproducible in Binder
text:
3.1 Task
Imagine that, instead of sending someone your analysis and asking them to install R, the right packages, system libraries, and other software, you could simply put the whole computer you used for the analysis in a box and post it to them. They could open the box, switch it on, and run the analysis in exactly the same environment. Of course, we cannot realistically post our laptops around every time we share an analysis—but this is roughly the idea behind containers. A container packages an application together with the software and system components it needs to run, providing a consistent environment across different computers.
Docker is one of the most widely used technologies for creating and running these containers. Instead of packaging an entire physical computer, Docker allows us to define a lightweight, reproducible computing environment containing things such as a particular version of R, R packages, system libraries, and other software required by the project. We can describe this environment in a Dockerfile, build it into a Docker image, and then run that image as a container. In this way, Docker extends what we have done with renv. Specifically, we can capture much more of the environment in which those packages and the analysis run as done previously.
Docker and Binder
In this workshop, we will use Docker together via Binder as one way of making a project easier for others to reproduce. Docker defines the computing environment, while Binder can take the project and its container configuration and make it available through a simple web browser! So, someone can launch the project without first installing R, configuring the required packages, or setting up Docker on their own computer. Magic!
However, Binder is not a solution for every project. Resources such as computing power and session time are limited, and Binder is generally better suited to interactive or educational projects. Still, full analysis examples are available out there accompanying published papers.
For this workshop, we will use Binder to run our Docker-based environment through a web browser, so participants do not need to install Docker or configure the environment locally. Running Docker directly on a computer is a more flexible option, particularly when you need more control or computing resources, but that workflow is beyond the scope of this tutorial.
Why do I need to learn about Docker?
You might reasonably ask: if renv and targets already make my R project reproducible, why do I need Docker? This is because reproducibility has several layers. renv helps us reproduce the R package environment, and targets helps us reproduce the analysis workflow, but neither necessarily captures everything installed on the computer. An analysis might also depend on a particular version of R, system libraries,etc.
Fro now, the important thing is to understand the basic idea: instead of asking someone to recreate your computing environment manually, you give them a description of that environment that can be used to recreate it automatically. Combined with renv and targets, this gives us a much more complete reproducible workflow.
This walks through the final Dockerfile used to publish rafavdz/reprod_workshop3 on mybinder.org, step by step.

text:
3.2 Instructions
You will continue working on your Rstudio project. If there was not enough time to complete the acitivites of the previosu step, you can download this completed R Project from GitHub, and pick it up from there.
Create a simple empty text file name Docker in your root directory.

3.2.1 Choose the base image
Start from the Rocker Project’s binder image, pinned to the exact R version recorded in renv.lock. Please check which version you are using.
FROM rocker/binder:4.4.1
In this case, we are not trying to recover an older workflow in R. So, no need to go back in time.
renv.lock records the R version the packages were snapshotted against, so the container’s R version and the lockfile’s R version need to match for renv::restore().

title: 3  Containers: Your own Git repository reproducible in Binder
section: 3.3 Install system libraries for spatial operations
text:
3.3 Install system libraries for spatial operations
The project uses sf/terra, which link against GDAL, GEOS, and PROJ at the C/C++ level. rocker/binder doesn’t include these by default (that’s only the rocker/geospatial family), so they’re installed manually. This has to happen as root, then the shell drops back to the regular container user for everything else.
USER root
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    libgdal-dev \
    gdal-bin \
    libgeos-dev \
    libproj-dev \
    libudunits2-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
USER ${NB_USER}
Without this step, renv::restore() either fails outright trying to compile sf/terra from source, or fails to find the headers it needs even if a source build is attempted.
rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* at the end isn’t strictly required, but it keeps the image smaller by discarding the package index Debian/Ubuntu downloaded for apt-get update.

title: 3  Containers: Your own Git repository reproducible in Binder
section: 3.5 Copy only the renv bootstrap files first
text:
3.5 Copy only the renv bootstrap files first
COPY --chown=${NB_USER} renv.lock renv.lock
COPY --chown=${NB_USER} .Rprofile .Rprofile
RUN mkdir -p renv
COPY --chown=${NB_USER} renv/activate.R renv/activate.R
COPY --chown=${NB_USER} renv/settings.json renv/settings.json
Here, Docker caches each instruction as a layer, and invalidates a layer (and everything after it) only when its inputs change. By copying just the four files renv actually needs to bootstrap itself — before copying the rest of the repository — the expensive package-restore step below only re-runs when renv.lock or renv’s own config changes. Editing an R script or a README later won’t force a full package reinstall on the next build.
--chown=${NB_USER} ensures these files are owned by the container’s regular user, not root. Otherwise, later R sessions running as rstudio could hit permission errors touching renv’s files.

title: 3  Containers: Your own Git repository reproducible in Binder
text:
3.6 Restore the R environment
RUN R -e "renv::restore()"
This installs every package pinned in renv.lock into renv’s own project-local library (not the system library). Two consequences of that choice, made deliberately for this repository:

renv stays active at runtime. Because .Rprofile and renv/activate.R are still present in the image, every new R session in the running container re-activates renv automatically — attaching the already-restored library, not reinstalling anything.
The lockfile stays visible and inspectable. Anyone inspecting this workflow can open renv.lock, run renv::status(), and see exactly what’s pinned, which is in line of a reproducibility workshop.

title: 3  Containers: Your own Git repository reproducible in Binder
text:
3.8 Declare how the container runs
EXPOSE 8888
CMD ["jupyter", "lab", "--ip", "0.0.0.0", "--no-browser"]
These two lines are inherited from the upstream rocker/binder image and are restated here for clarity. Binder’s infrastructure expects a Jupyter server listening on 8888, which is what actually gets launched. RStudio isn’t started by a separate CMD; it’s reached through jupyter-rsession-proxy, which routes a browser request at a specific path through to an rserver process the image already knows how to start. That’s what the launch URL takes care of next.

title: 3  Containers: Your own Git repository reproducible in Binder
text:
3.9 Final Dockerfile
So your final Docker file should look as following:
FROM rocker/binder:4.4.1

# --- system libraries for sf/terra ---
USER root
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    libgdal-dev \
    gdal-bin \
    libgeos-dev \
    libproj-dev \
    libudunits2-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
USER ${NB_USER}

WORKDIR ${HOME}

# --- copy only the renv bootstrap files first (better build-cache reuse) ---
COPY --chown=${NB_USER} renv.lock renv.lock
COPY --chown=${NB_USER} .Rprofile .Rprofile
RUN mkdir -p renv
COPY --chown=${NB_USER} renv/activate.R renv/activate.R
COPY --chown=${NB_USER} renv/settings.json renv/settings.json

# --- restore into renv's own project library (kept active at runtime) ---
RUN R -e "renv::restore()"

# --- now copy the rest of the repository ---
COPY --chown=${NB_USER} . ${HOME}

EXPOSE 8888
CMD ["jupyter", "lab", "--ip", "0.0.0.0", "--no-browser"]
Save this in your project.

3.9.1 Add the Launch-in-Binder badge
Add the following in your README.md
[![Binder](https://mybinder.org/badge_logo.svg)](https://mybinder.org/v2/gh/rafavdz/reprod_workshop3/main?urlpath=rstudio)
This gives anyone visiting the repository a one-click route into a running RStudio session with the environment already restored.
Now, make sure to commit your changes, and push them.
